newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil supply boom spells end for crude rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil supply boom spells end for crude rally.

text.p: A tidal wave of oil from all corners of the globe is beginning to catch up with robust demand, swelling stocks and pointing to lower crude prices later in the year, analysts said on Friday.

Supply from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) surged to 26.9 million barrels per day (bpd) in January, a million bpd above 1996's average and well in excess of the cartel's long-ignored 25.03 million ceiling, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.

"That's a big number and it confirms my view that OPEC output will go through 27 million bpd by April or May. I suspect it will be nearer 27.5 million by the end of the year," said Mehdi Varzi at finance house Kleinwort Benson.

Shrugging off delays and lower than expected growth in 1996, producers outside OPEC should lift output two million bpd to 45.5 million bpd this year, the Paris-based IEA said in its latest monthly report.

"Although considerably less than expected, the growth in world oil supply in the last three months of 1996 and in January has been substantial and appears to have established strong upward trends in OPEC as well as non-OPEC production," it said.

Analysts said rising supply from a range of sources including Iraq, which pumped 1.1 million bpd in January, the first full month of a U.N. oil-for-food programme allowing Baghdad to export for the first time in six years, would boost global oil inventories despite booming demand.
The IEA increased its estimate for world demand in 1997 by 100,000 bpd to 73.7 million bpd, a rise of 1.9 million bpd over 1996.

"Even if the IEA is half a million barrels optimistic about supply, it won't make any difference. There will still be a surplus by the second half of the year," said Geoff Pyne, energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.
"Everybody's focusing on non-OPEC, but the growth in OPEC output is also accelerating and that can't be good for prices," he added.

International benchmark Brent crude oil, trading 18 cents lower at $21.51 a barrel on Friday, has shed $1 this week as fears of a winter heating fuel shortage evaporated in the face of warmer than normal temperatures in the key consuming markets of Europe and the United States.

Distillate stocks, including heating oil and diesel, in the leading industrial nations, ended 1996 12 million barrels higher than a year earlier, the first year-on-year surplus for 19 months. Total industry stocks were still 28 million barrels in arrears but this was the lowest shortfall since July 1995, the IEA said.
Nevertheless, Brent remains ahead of its 1996 average of $20.30 a barrel and is unlikely to collapse in the short-term as refiners raise gasoline output before the peak summer driving season.

"We really are in a demand boom which should limit the downside at least over the next two years.. but assuming we see the big rise in non-OPEC output, prices should return to the $18-20 range by mid-year," said Kleinwort Benson's Varzi.
Analysts say the world oil market could be entering a prolonged period of oversupply after an extended rally which took prices near six-year highs last year.
"The market lacks an adjustment mechanism. In the past if prices were high OPEC would leak extra barrels and if they were low they would cut (output)," said Pyne at UBS.
"They can't leak because most are producing at sustainable capacity and they won't cut," he said.
Ambitious investment in production capacity expansion and a campaign to woo foreign investors has led most OPEC producers to ignore their quotas.
